paragraphs.heading: Land where trees give up
paragraphs.text: A tundra is a biome in which bitter cold and short growing seasons hold trees back. There are three kinds: Arctic, Alpine and Antarctic. The plant cover is made up of dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens, though scattered trees grow in some tundra areas. The border zone where tundra meets forest is called the tree line or timberline.

paragraphs.heading: Frozen ground below
paragraphs.text: The word usually means land whose subsoil is permafrost, ground that stays frozen all the time. Arctic tundra is frozen for much of the year, and its soil is frozen from 25 to 90 cm down, which makes it impossible for trees to grow. In summer the top layer thaws and the ground turns soggy, dotted with marshes, lakes, bogs and streams. The frozen layer underneath stops the meltwater from sinking deeper, so it pools at the surface instead.

paragraphs.heading: Cold, windy and dry
paragraphs.text: Polar tundra has two main seasons, winter and summer. Winters are cold, dark and windy, averaging around −28 °C and sometimes reaching −50 °C. Summer days usually warm to about 12 °C but often fall to 3 °C or even below freezing. Winds often blow at 50–100 km/h. The tundra also counts as a polar desert, with only about 150–250 mm of precipitation a year, but little water evaporates either.

paragraphs.heading: Who lives there
paragraphs.text: Few kinds of living things manage here. There are about 1,700 species of vascular plants and only 48 land mammal species, plus a few fish, though millions of birds arrive each year for the marshes. Animals include reindeer, musk ox, Arctic hare, Arctic fox, snowy owl, lemmings and mosquitoes, with polar bears near the ocean, while animals like frogs and lizards are largely missing. People live here too, mostly nomadic reindeer herders such as the Nenets and Nganasan.

paragraphs.heading: A carbon store at risk
paragraphs.text: Tundra soil is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, and its permafrost holds a great deal of dead plant matter stored as methane and carbon dioxide. That makes the soil a carbon sink, a store of carbon. As global warming thaws the ground, these greenhouse gases escape into the air, which adds to climate change in a feedback loop. Thawing also threatens roads and pipelines built on frozen ground, and it could change which species can survive there.

paragraphs.heading: Fire on the tundra
paragraphs.text: Fire is part of the picture too. Research in Alaska found that fires return about every 150 to 200 years, with drier lowlands burning more often than wetter highlands. Where dead plants and peat pile up, wildfire becomes a risk: in 2007, 1,039 km² of tundra burned on the north slope of Alaska's Brooks Range. Fires like this can both result from global warming and feed it.
